claims.text: Enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings is governed by chemically complex interfaces.
Chemically complex interfaces act as effective barriers to dislocation motion.
Blocking dislocation motion at the interfaces delays creep mechanisms.
The initial coatings are as-deposited, nanostructured multilayers with alternating layers and chemically distinct interfaces.
A controlled comparison between coatings with complex interfaces and a homogeneous HEA or simplified-interface multilayer can reveal the role of interface chemistry.
Creep becomes pronounced under prolonged loading at elevated temperature and comparable stress.
Chemical complexity and nanoscale layer thickness impede dislocation transmission across interfaces.
Dislocations generated under stress are blocked or slowed at the layer interfaces.
Blocking dislocations at the interfaces reduces strain localization and the progression of creep deformation.
Interrupting dislocation glide at complex interfaces increases the activation energy for creep.
Complex-interface multilayers will exhibit significantly lower creep strain over time than the baseline.
Complex-interface multilayers will exhibit less dislocation accumulation in localized zones than the baseline.
Complex-interface multilayers will exhibit less strain localization than the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies at elevated temperature and moderate-to-high stress where creep is dominant.
Prominent interface effects require nanoscale layer thickness and adequate interface quality.
The magnitude of creep-resistance improvement may depend on microstructure, composition, and processing history.
A lack of statistically significant differences in creep strain, dislocation accumulation, and strain localization across repeated tests would refute the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mediator says interfaces promote dislocation pile-up, whereas the predicted outcome expects reduced dislocation accumulation and the experiment specifically measures accumulation near interfaces. The hypothesis does not clarify whether increased interfacial pile-up is expected alongside reduced accumulation elsewhere.
